title: Waiting for the rth Success
short: The number of trials needed for r successes has P(X = k) = C(k − 1, r − 1) pʳ (1 − p)^(k − r) and mean r/p.
trouble: Students use C(k, r) instead of C(k − 1, r − 1), forgetting that the last trial must be the rth success.

blocks.html: The geometric distribution counts the trials up to the first success. Waiting for the third success, or the fifth, gives the negative binomial distribution. As in that lesson, $X$ counts all the trials, including the last success. (Some books count only the failures, $X - r$; the ideas are the same.)

In independent trials with success probability $p$, the number of trials $X$ needed for the $r$th success has $$P(X = k) = \binom{k - 1}{r - 1}p^{r}(1 - p)^{k - r}, \quad k = r, r + 1, \ldots,$$ with $E[X] = \frac{r}{p}$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X) = \frac{r(1 - p)}{p^{2}}$.

$X = k$ means trial $k$ is a success and the first $k - 1$ trials contain exactly $r - 1$ successes, in any of $\binom{k - 1}{r - 1}$ arrangements. Each arrangement has $r$ successes and $k - r$ failures, probability $p^{r}(1 - p)^{k - r}$. For the mean, split the wait into $r$ stages: trials to the first success, then from there to the second, and so on. Each stage is geometric with mean $\frac{1}{p}$, so by linearity $E[X] = \frac{r}{p}$. The stages are independent, so their variances $\frac{1 - p}{p^{2}}$ add too.

blocks.title: Coins
blocks.q: Flip a fair coin until the 3rd head. Find the probability that exactly 5 flips are needed.
steps: The 5th flip is the 3rd head, and the first 4 flips hold exactly 2 heads: $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ arrangements.

blocks.title: Sixes
blocks.q: Roll a die until the 2nd six. Find $P(X = 4)$ and $E[X]$.

blocks.title: A best-of-seven series
blocks.q: Team A wins each game with probability $0.6$, independently. In a best-of-seven series (first to 4 wins), find the probability that A wins in exactly 6 games.
steps: Game 6 must be A's 4th win, and games 1 to 5 hold exactly 3 A-wins: $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ arrangements.

blocks.html: "The $r$th success comes on or before trial $m$" is the same event as "at least $r$ successes in the first $m$ trials". So you can add the negative binomial probabilities for $k = r, \ldots, m$, or add binomial probabilities for $r$ or more successes in $m$ trials. Both give the same number, a useful check.

Using $\binom{k}{r}$ instead of $\binom{k - 1}{r - 1}$. The last trial is not free: it must be the $r$th success, so only the earlier $k - 1$ trials can be arranged. Check with $r = 1$: the formula must give the geometric $p(1 - p)^{k - 1}$, and $\binom{k - 1}{0} = 1$ does.
